alignment.note: The Greek negative particle οὐκ and Latin non are discrete words, whereas Syriac fuses the conjunction and negation into the single proclitic form ܘܠܐ ('and not'); the same Syriac token thus serves both the coordinating and negating function.

Greek ἤφιεν is a synthetic imperfect of ἀφίημι ('was permitting'); Latin sinebat matches it with a single imperfect. Syriac renders the durative past periphrastically with the perfect ܫܒܩ plus the auxiliary ܗܘܐ, a standard Aramaic construction for continuous past action.

Greek ἵνα τις and Latin ut quisquam keep the conjunction and indefinite pronoun separate, whereas Syriac contracts the relative-conjunction and the noun ܐܢܫ ('a person/anyone') into the single token ܕܐܢܫ, so the indefinite subject and subordinator share one form.

Greek expresses motion 'through' with διά plus the genitive article τοῦ; Latin uses the simple preposition per without an article; Syriac employs the compound locative ܒܓܘ ('within/in the midst of'), which shifts the nuance from passage 'through' toward movement 'inside' the precinct.

The Clementine Vulgate closes the clause with a colon, marking continuation into the following teaching; neither the Greek (which ends with a full stop here) nor the Syriac carries an equivalent discourse-level punctuation mark at this point.
